title: The Five-Burner Theory
contributor: A woman in tech, learning to tend her stove
pullQuote: Success isn't about a five-alarm fire. It's about the agility to move the heat where it's needed most.

paragraphs: I sat in the glow of my dual monitors at a Big Tech campus, staring at a cooling cup of coffee and realizing why I felt so thin. A woman's life is a stove with five burners: Work, Marriage, Kids, Fitness, and Social Life.
The reality? You can only keep two on high heat to truly excel.

sections.heading: The Seasonal Shift
paragraphs: Last quarter, my Work burner was roaring. I was pushing code for a global launch and navigating cross-functional politics. To survive the pace, I kept Fitness on high. I was productive and athletic — but the other burners suffered.
Marriage was on a low simmer. We were passing ships. Social Life? Stone cold — I was a ghost in the group chat. The kids were getting the distracted version of Mom.
When the product finally shipped, I looked at the stove. Keeping the Work flame that high had been scorching everything else.

sections.heading: The Trade-Off
paragraphs: I've stopped trying to ignite the whole range. Now I consciously adjust the dials. I turned Work down to a steady glow. I clicked Kids and Marriage to high heat. Fitness moved to a maintenance simmer.

sections.heading: The Bottom Line
paragraphs: In the high-pressure world of tech, the 'have it all' myth is a recipe for burnout. Success isn't about a five-alarm fire — it's about the agility to move the heat where it's needed most. If you smell something burning, it's time to check your knobs.
Which two burners are getting your energy tonight?

whatLearned: That keeping the Work flame too high scorches everything else — and that consciously adjusting the dials is not giving up. It's wisdom.
